title: Three claims, one broken crate
subtitle: The Nur’s factor has asked the weighers to take three crates of glass flasks out of the sale assessment. He carries a bowl of broken glass from clerk to clerk. Mariam of Cambay asks you to check the crates themselves before consigning them to her storeroom.

evidence.label: 01  Manifest
evidence.title: The Nur’s declaration
evidence.text:
Nur — nau from Cambay
Glass consignment received in Melaka by Mariam of Cambay.

Glass beads: 8 bundles for sale.
Empty blue glass flasks: crates 1 through 6, 12 flasks per crate. Sound crates: 200 each.

Amended by the ship’s factor: crates 2, 4 and 5 are all broken and contain no saleable flasks. Only crates 1, 3 and 6 are entered at the sound price. The beads are unchanged.

evidence.label: 02  First tally
evidence.title: What can be seen on deck
evidence.text:
Weights: all six crates are aboard. Crate 2 is slightly lighter than the others. Glass and its fragments both weigh something, the weigher says; without lifting the lids he cannot say what was lost overboard or what is still whole.

A corner of crate 2 is crushed. Crates 4 and 5 have no visible damage. The factor carries the bowl of shards with him when he leads the clerk from one crate to the next.

evidence.label: 03  Testimony
evidence.title: Whose shards are these?
evidence.text:
Factor: The glass broke in three crates when we set them down too hard. I took a handful from each. It is all one colour; there's no point carrying three bowls.

Porter: Number two slipped while we were shifting it. The factor sent me forward before he opened anything. When I came back he wanted four and five left beside the hatch for a buyer’s boat.

Mariam: I’ll answer for every sound flask that comes through my door. Open the crates here, where the clerk can see them.

evidence.label: 04  Lift the lids
evidence.title: The bowl and the flasks
evidence.text: Opened: crate 2 is full of broken glass. A piece of thick blue rim in the factor’s bowl fits a chipped neck still wedged in the straw. Crates 4 and 5 each hold twelve intact blue flasks, wrapped separately, with no loose chips among the straw. The other three crates and the eight bundles of beads agree with the declaration.

rulings.label: Major Fraud — hold the suspect cargo
Story Event — hold the ship and notify the court

reasons.label: The shards match crate 2; crates 4 and 5 hold the sound flasks the factor meant to land without assessment.
The bowl establishes that the glass in all three crates broke.
The weight of each crate proves whether its flasks are broken.

feedback_by_method.marks: The crate numbers identify the lots, not which flasks broke. An unmarked blow can still break glass.
feedback_by_method.measurements: Whole flasks and their fragments can weigh the same. The readings cannot show that two of the claims are false.
feedback_by_method.testimony: The porter saw one crate dropped, but did not see inside the others. Open both disputed crates before accusing the factor.
feedback_by_method.manifest: The factor’s amendment names the three claims. It does not prove the claims or identify where the shards came from.

hidden_truth.success: In the temenggung’s name, you set aside crates 4 and 5 for his judgement and refuse the factor’s false amendment. Crate 2 really did break. Mariam recounts the whole flasks with the weighers and can take the rest into storage. At settlement the office recovers 28 on the restored value of 400: 24 in entry dues and 4 in weighing fees.
hidden_truth.clear: The Nur is cleared at the amended value. A buyer’s boat takes sound flasks out of crates entered as broken.
hidden_truth.unsupported: That evidence does not support an amendment in the temenggung’s name. The false breakage claims stand, and two crates of sound glass escape assessment.
hidden_truth.hold: You hold the whole Nur for the court instead of bringing the suspect crates before the customs bench. The court’s men find a false valuation, not a matter of state. The bead and flask buyers leave without a sale.

truth.summary: The factor uses genuine damage to crate 2 to support false duty-reducing claims on two crates intended for sale. Mariam challenges the claims.
deduction: The factor says he took shards from three crates and has removed all three from the sale value.
A piece from his bowl fits a broken flask in crate 2. Neither of the other crates contains shards, and both still hold their full allotment of intact flasks.
The factor set the sound crates aside for a buyer, not the rubbish heap. Restore the value of crates 4 and 5 but do not assess the genuinely broken crate as sound.

history_notes.note: Pires lists glass vessels and beads in the trade through Cambay. Packing fragile flasks with cushioning is plausible; see docs/research/commodities.md §3.13 and docs/research/seals-marks-packaging.md §4.

The shahbandar rules in the temenggung’s name. The per-lot valuation, damage adjustment and 6-plus-1 calculation are gameplay simplifications, not documented Gujarati assessment procedure; Pires notes Gujarati whole-ship valuation (docs/research/port-official.md §§5–6).
The incident and prices are invented. Written manifests, cargo seals and merchant-mark registers are gameplay inventions (docs/research/seals-marks-packaging.md §§1–3).
